claims.claim: The marketing mix is the set of marketing tools a firm blends to reach its target market — classically the four Ps of product, price, place, and promotion; the elements are the firm's own controllable decisions, while competitors and the economy are outside the mix.

The term 'marketing mix' was popularized by Neil Borden, a Harvard advertising professor, in the 1950s and set out in his 1964 article 'The Concept of the Marketing Mix'; E. Jerome McCarthy refined the ideas and named the classic four Ps, popularized through his 1960 book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

The marketing mix is created after a firm has defined its target market, and every target market requires a unique marketing mix to satisfy the needs of the target customers and meet the firm's goals.

The marketing mix is only as good as its weakest part, and a successful marketing mix requires careful tailoring; the four Ps interact significantly with each other rather than working as independent decisions.

The extended marketing mix adds people, process, and physical evidence to the classic four Ps — an expansion recommended for services, where direct interaction with service providers and the service environment shape the customer's experience.

Marketers adjust the elements of the mix — packaging, after-sales service, warranties, price range, distribution, and promotion — as objectives and market conditions change, including expanding into new markets.
The heart of the marketing mix is the good, service, or idea (the product), but the product alone is not the mix; the mix only succeeds when the other elements support it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number of Ps: some textbooks teach four Ps, OpenStax's Introduction to Business refers to 'the 5Ps discussed earlier' in its marketing-mix section, and the services extension is commonly taught as seven Ps.
positions: Classic four Ps (product, price, place, promotion) — the Borden/McCarthy tradition (CFI, Investopedia)
A five-P version counting people appears in some survey texts (OpenStax Introduction to Business)
The seven-P extension: the classic four plus people, process, and physical evidence, for services (CFI, Investopedia)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the classic four Ps as the standard framework and names the seven-P extension as the recognized services version, following CFI and Investopedia. The OpenStax '5Ps' reference is not adopted; the lesson avoids claiming a single official count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the mix's elements are best described as 'controllable' tools.
positions: Classic textbook phrasing: the mix is the set of controllable marketing tools the firm blends (Kotler tradition, reproduced in many textbooks)
Descriptive explainers simply call the mix a set of tools a company uses to influence consumers (CFI)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the definition to the standard textbook tradition and describes the four Ps as tools the firm chooses — its own decisions — while noting that external forces (competitors, the economy) sit outside the mix. No source is quoted verbatim on this phrasing.
